Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Vignette:
Mr. Tran, a 47-year-old South Eastern Asian married man and park ranger, experienced a traumatic event that has significantly impacted his daily life and well-being. The trauma stemmed from a life-threatening illness of his child five years ago, an experience that continues to haunt him. The incident began during what was supposed to be a routine visit to the hospital for his daughter’s asthma check-up. Suddenly, her condition worsened, leading to an emergency admission and several days in intensive care. The antiseptic smell and the sterile environment of the hospital remain potent triggers for Mr. Tran, evoking vivid memories of that harrowing time. In those weeks, Mr. Tran found himself constantly on edge, feeling dizzy or lightheaded as if his world were spinning out of control. This dizziness often hit him at work, where he would suddenly feel disoriented and unable to focus on his tasks. The smell of alcohol, which reminded him of the sanitizing agents used in hospitals, also triggered these episodes. Following the traumatic event, Mr. Tran began to ruminate about what could have been done differently. He frequently thought about how to get even with those he perceived as responsible for his child’s illness, a pattern of revenge fantasies that kept him preoccupied and anxious. Additionally, he often dwelled on what other people had done to him, feeling a sense of injustice that fueled his negative emotions. Avoiding reminders of the event became another coping mechanism. He found it particularly challenging when colleagues at work talked about their own children’s health issues or when he had to visit the hospital for any reason. These situations made him feel uncomfortable and agitated, prompting him to avoid such conversations and places altogether. Over time, these avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships both at home and at work. He became increasingly withdrawn from social interactions, which led to misunderstandings with his wife who found him distant and uncommunicative. At work, he missed several important meetings and failed to complete tasks that required collaboration, resulting in some tension with his colleagues. Despite these challenges, Mr. Tran continued to manage the daily responsibilities of being a park ranger but often felt overwhelmed by the cumulative stress. The constant fear of something happening again made it difficult for him to focus on his duties or enjoy simple pleasures in life. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was an incident where he almost had an accident at work due to dizziness, narrowly avoiding a serious injury. This close call shook him deeply and made him realize the need to address these lingering effects of trauma. He is most afraid that his child might relapse into another life-threatening illness, but he also hopes for relief from the constant fear and anxiety that has been ruling his thoughts and actions. In therapy, Mr. Tran seeks to better understand and manage his reactions to triggers, reduce rumination, and find healthier ways to cope with reminders of the traumatic event. He is determined to reclaim a sense of control over his life and work towards healing from this deeply distressing experience.
